question: M1
answer:
BASICMED AIRCRAFT LIMITS — UNITED STATES (current law, in force on or after 12 November 2024)

1. ANSWER TABLE

| Limit | Value | Regulatory hook |
|---|---|---|
| Maximum certificated takeoff weight (MTOW) | 12,500 lb | 14 CFR 61.113(i)(1); FESSA sec. 2307(j) as amended by PL 118-63 sec. 828(a)(4) |
| Maximum occupants the aircraft may be AUTHORIZED to carry | 7 (including any required flightcrew members) | 14 CFR 61.113(i)(1); 14 CFR 91.319(j) for experimental |
| Maximum passengers on board | 6 (persons other than the pilot operating under BasicMed) | 14 CFR 61.113(i)(2)/(i)(1) per FESSA sec. 2307(a)(8)(A) as amended |

2. SOURCE TEXT (verbatim, current)

- FAA, BasicMed airmen page: "Any aircraft authorized under federal law to carry not more than 7 occupants; Has a maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds ... Carries not more than six passengers."
- Federal Register, final rule published 18 Nov 2024 (2024-26935): "Increase the number of allowable passengers from 5 to 6 and occupants from 6 to 7 for covered aircraft; Increase the maximum takeoff weight from 6,000 pounds to 12,500 pounds for covered aircraft ..." and "a covered aircraft may now be authorized to carry up to 7 occupants (including any required flight crewmembers) and may be operating with up to 6 passengers on board."
- FAA Notice N 8000.386 (14 Nov 2024): "Per PL 118-63, Section 828, Expansion of BasicMed, the following aircraft limitations will apply on or after November 12, 2024: The aircraft is authorized to carry no more than seven occupants, The aircraft has an MTOW of no more than 12,500 pounds, and The aircraft is operated with no more than six passengers on board."

3. DEFINITIONS AND HOW TO APPLY EACH FIGURE

3.1 MTOW = maximum CERTIFICATED takeoff weight. It is the weight established in the aircraft's design approval — type certificate (TC), supplemental type certificate (STC), or amended TC (ATC) — not the actual takeoff weight on a given day and not maximum landing weight or maximum zero-fuel weight. For experimental aircraft issued a Special Airworthiness Certificate, the MTOW is the maximum gross weight in the FAA-approved operating limitations / weight-and-balance data. A type-certificated aircraft whose design approval MTOW exceeds 12,500 lb does not qualify, even if it is flown below 12,500 lb; conversely, an aircraft altered by STC/ATC to a certificated MTOW of 12,500 lb or less does qualify (AC 68-1A sec. 5.1.2 rationale, applied to the amended thresholds).

3.2 Occupants (7) = the number the aircraft is AUTHORIZED under Federal law to carry, including the pilot and any required flightcrew members. This is a property of the aircraft's design approval / operating limitations, not of how many seats are installed or how many people happen to be on board. An aircraft certificated for 8 or more occupants is ineligible for BasicMed even if it is flown with 7 or fewer aboard. (The classic pre-2024 example — Piper PA-32/PA-34 variants certificated for more than the occupant cap — remains the correct analytical method; only the cap number changed.)

3.3 Passengers (6) = persons on board other than the pilot operating under BasicMed. Consistent with AC 68-1A sec. 5.2.1-5.2.2: an occupant other than the BasicMed PIC may be (a) a passenger, (b) a required pilot flightcrew member where the aircraft is certificated for more than one pilot or the regulations require more than one pilot, or (c) a flight instructor giving instruction. A pilot riding along who is neither required crew nor an instructing CFI counts as a PASSENGER.

3.4 Arithmetic consistency of the three limits: 7 occupants − 1 BasicMed PIC = 6 passengers, so a single-pilot aircraft can be filled to both caps simultaneously. In a two-pilot-crew aircraft, 7 occupants − 2 required flightcrew = 5 passengers, which is below the 6-passenger cap, so the occupant limit binds first. Neither cap can be satisfied by exceeding the other.

4. SECONDARY ELIGIBILITY CONDITION (aircraft)

Aircraft that are transport category rotorcraft certificated to airworthiness standards under 14 CFR part 29 are excluded from the definition of 'covered aircraft' (PL 118-63 sec. 828(a)(4); implemented in 61.113(i)(1) and 91.319(j)).

5. SCOPE NOTE — WHAT THESE NUMBERS ARE NOT

These are per-flight aircraft and operating limits on the pilot exercising BasicMed privileges; they are independent of the pilot's medical history, of the CMEC, and of the online course, which live in 14 CFR part 68 and 61.23(c)(3). Part 68 itself contains no weight or seat-count number — the aircraft limits are in Part 61. The other BasicMed operating limits (at or below 18,000 ft MSL, within the US or another authorizing country, indicated airspeed not above 250 knots, not for compensation or hire) are outside the three asks and are listed here only so the boundary of the answer is explicit. The limits apply to the entire flight, takeoff to touchdown, and the aircraft must still be operated within its own operating limitations where those are more restrictive.

6. SUPERSEDED VALUES — DO NOT USE

Before 12 November 2024 the limits were: MTOW 6,000 lb; not more than 6 occupants; not more than 5 passengers. Those figures still appear in older FAA material — AC 68-1A (2020), the July/August 2017 FAA Safety Briefing, and the 'BasicMed One Departure' chart (1 MAY 17) — all of which predate the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 and are superseded on these three numbers. Any answer citing 6,000 lb / 6 / 5 as current is out of date.

7. CITATIONS

- 14 CFR 61.113(i)(1) (covered aircraft and passenger limits), 61.113(i)(2) (operating limits); 14 CFR 91.319(j) (experimental aircraft occupant limit).
- FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024, PL 118-63, sec. 828 (amending FESSA sec. 2307, 49 U.S.C. 44703 note).
- FAA Final Rule, 89 FR (18 Nov 2024), docket text 2024-26935.
- FAA Notice N 8000.386, 'BasicMed for Examiners' (14 Nov 2024), para. 5(a).
- FAA BasicMed airmen certification webpage (current).
- AC 68-1A, 'BasicMed' (methodology for determining authorized occupancy and MTOW; numerical examples therein are pre-amendment).

question: M2
answer:
CURRENT U.S. NATIONAL PRIMARY AMBIENT AIR QUALITY STANDARDS FOR PM2.5
(as of the most recent regulatory information retrieved, 2026-11-23)

1. ANSWER TABLE — PRIMARY (HEALTH-BASED) PM2.5 STANDARDS

| # | Averaging time | Level | Units | Form (statistical test for compliance) | Regulatory cite | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Annual | 9.0 | µg/m³ | Annual arithmetic mean concentration, averaged over 3 years, at each monitor; standard is met when the 3-year average of annual arithmetic means is ≤ 9.0 µg/m³ (40 CFR Part 50, App. N) | 40 CFR 50.18, as revised by the 2024 PM NAAQS reconsideration (89 FR 16202, Mar. 6, 2024; effective May 6, 2024) | In effect; revised downward from 12.0 µg/m³ |
| 2 | 24-hour | 35 | µg/m³ | 98th percentile of 24-hour concentrations, averaged over 3 years, at each monitor; standard is met when the 3-year average of annual 98th-percentile values is ≤ 35 µg/m³ (40 CFR Part 50, App. N) | 40 CFR 50.13(c) | In effect; retained unchanged in the 2024 reconsideration |

Headline: annual primary PM2.5 = 9.0 µg/m³; 24-hour primary PM2.5 = 35 µg/m³.

2. WHAT 'CURRENT' MEANS HERE

- Governing action: EPA's final reconsideration of the PM NAAQS, signed February 7, 2024, published March 6, 2024 (89 FR 16202), effective May 6, 2024 (60 days after publication).
- That rule set the level of the primary (health-based) annual PM2.5 standard at 9.0 µg/m³ and expressly did not change the primary 24-hour PM2.5 standard (35 µg/m³), the secondary annual PM2.5 standard (15.0 µg/m³), or the primary/secondary 24-hour PM10 standard (150 µg/m³).
- Any answer dated before May 6, 2024 would instead be 12.0 µg/m³ annual (2012 standard) / 35 µg/m³ 24-hour. The 9.0 / 35 pair is the correct present-day answer.
- Implementation status (not a change to the levels): EPA's designations page, last updated October 2, 2026, describes the revised 2024 annual standard as in effect and reports that EPA gave notice of its intended approach for finalizing initial designations. Designations affect implementation timing (attainment dates, SIP obligations), not the numeric levels above.

3. LEVEL vs. FORM — WHY BOTH ARE GIVEN

A NAAQS has five elements: indicator, averaging time, level, form, and primary/secondary class. The 'level' is the number requested; the 'form' is how monitoring data are reduced to a value compared against that level. Stating 9.0 µg/m³ without the form would not define compliance. Both forms use 3-year averaging under Appendix N to 40 CFR Part 50:
- Annual: 3-year average of annual arithmetic means ≤ 9.0 µg/m³.
- 24-hour: 3-year average of annual 98th-percentile 24-hour values ≤ 35 µg/m³.

4. SECONDARY STANDARDS (OUT OF SCOPE BUT NOTED TO PREVENT CONFUSION)

Secondary (welfare-based) PM2.5 standards, retained in 2024: annual 15.0 µg/m³ (annual arithmetic mean, 3-year average) and 24-hour 35 µg/m³ (98th percentile, 3-year average). The 15.0 µg/m³ figure appears in the same regulatory section as the 24-hour standard and is the most common source of mix-up with the primary annual level — it is NOT the current primary annual level.

5. SOURCE RECONCILIATION (documented discrepancy and its resolution)

- EPA, 'Final Reconsideration of the NAAQS for PM' (epa.gov/pm-pollution/final-reconsideration-national-ambient-air-quality-standards-particulate-matter-pm): 'EPA is setting the level of the primary (health-based) annual PM2.5 standard at 9.0 micrograms per cubic meter.' → supports 9.0.
- EPA, 2024 PM NAAQS Final Overview presentation, 'Summary of Previous Standards and 2024 Final Decision' table: Annual / Primary / 12.0 µg/m³ → 'Revise level to 9.0 µg/m³'; 24-hour / Primary and Secondary / 35 µg/m³ / 98th percentile, averaged over 3 years → 'Retain'. → supports 9.0 and 35, and supplies the forms.
- EPA, Particle Pollution Designations for the 2024 Revised Annual PM2.5 NAAQS: 'strengthening the standard from 12.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m3) to 9.0 µg/m3; retained the existing 24-hour PM2.5 standard at 35 µg/m3.' → supports 9.0 and 35.
- eCFR 40 CFR 50.13 (retrieved text): shows '15.0 µg/m³ annual arithmetic mean concentration, and 35 µg/m³ 24-hour average concentration' with the 1997/2006 amendment history. The 35 µg/m³ agrees. The 15.0 µg/m³ is the legacy provision in §50.13 — the retained 1997 secondary annual standard — not the current primary annual standard. The 2012 primary annual standard was codified in §50.18 at 12.0 µg/m³, and the 2024 rule revised that section to 9.0 µg/m³. Reading §50.13(a) alone therefore under-reports the primary annual standard; the EPA rule documents control.
- Net: 24-hour = 35 µg/m³ is unanimous across all sources; annual primary = 9.0 µg/m³ per the three EPA sources that describe the 2024 revision, with the 15.0 µg/m³ in §50.13 identified as the secondary annual standard.

6. VERIFICATION CHECKS PERFORMED

- Direction of change: 9.0 < 12.0 < 15.0, consistent with EPA's characterization of 'strengthening' the annual standard; a value above 12.0 would have been an error.
- Units: both standards are mass-concentration in µg/m³; no ppb/ppm conversion applies to PM2.5 (a gravimetric/mass indicator), so no unit conversion step exists that could introduce error.
- Internal consistency: the deliverable sets no numeric threshold other than the two standard levels themselves, so no stated value can violate a bound stated elsewhere in the deliverable.
- Scope: primary standards only are reported as the answer; secondary values appear solely as a labeled disambiguation note.

7. CITATIONS

- 40 CFR 50.13, 50.18 (eCFR, Title 40, Part 50).
- 89 FR 16202 (Mar. 6, 2024), Reconsideration of the National Ambient Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter.
- EPA, Final Reconsideration of the NAAQS for PM (web page).
- EPA, 2024 PM NAAQS Final Overview presentation (Feb. 2024).
- EPA, Particle Pollution Designations for the 2024 Revised Annual PM2.5 NAAQS (last updated Oct. 2, 2026).

The first reads: "(a) The national primary and secondary ambient air quality standards for particulate matter are 15.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m3) annual arithmetic mean concentration, and 35 µg/m3 24-hour average concentration measured in the ambient"

question: M3
answer:
# Hours-of-Service Limits — Driver of a Passenger-Carrying CMV (e.g., Motorcoach)

**Controlling authority:** 49 CFR § 395.5, *Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles* (applicability via 49 CFR § 390.3(a): the subchapter-B rules apply to all employers, employees, and CMVs that transport property **or passengers in interstate commerce**).

## 1. Direct answers (quick-reference card)

| # | Question | Answer | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | How many hours may the driver drive? | **10 hours** of driving time following 8 consecutive hours off duty | § 395.5(a)(1) |
| 2 | After how many consecutive hours off duty may the driver drive? | **8 consecutive hours** off duty | § 395.5(a)(1) and (a)(2) |
| 3 | After how many hours on duty may the driver no longer drive? | **15 hours** on duty following 8 consecutive hours off duty | § 395.5(a)(2) |

**Supplementary (not an answer to asks 1–3, but binding on the same driver):** no driving after **60 hours on duty in any 7 consecutive days** (carrier does not operate CMVs every day of the week) or **70 hours on duty in any 8 consecutive days** (carrier operates CMVs every day of the week) — § 395.5(b)(1)–(2). These are cumulative caps on *on-duty* time, separate from and in addition to the 10- and 15-hour daily limits.

## 2. The regulation text relied on

> **§ 395.5 Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles.**
> Subject to the exceptions and exemptions in § 395.1:
> (a) No motor carrier shall permit or require any driver used by it to drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle, nor shall any such driver drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle:
> (1) More than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty; or
> (2) For any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty.
> (b) No motor carrier shall permit or require a driver of a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle to drive, nor shall any driver drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle, **regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services**, for any period after—
> (1) Having been on duty 60 hours in any 7 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier does not operate commercial motor vehicles every day of the week; or
> (2) Having been on duty 70 hours in any period of 8 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier operates commercial motor vehicles every day of the week.

Source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-49/section-395.5 (70 FR 50073, Aug. 25, 2005).

FMCSA restates the same three limits in its carrier guidance:

> "No motor carrier of passengers shall permit or require any passenger-carrying CMV driver to drive: • More than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty, or • For any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty."

Source: https://www.fmcsa.dot.gov/safety/carrier-safety/hours-service-motor-carriers-passengers

## 3. ⚠ Correction to a common (and costly) default: passenger ≠ property

The property-carrying limits under **§ 395.3** are **11 hours driving / 10 consecutive hours off duty / 14-hour driving window**, plus a 30-minute break requirement. **Those numbers do not apply to a passenger-carrying CMV.** For passengers the figures are **10 / 8 / 15**. Any compliance document, dispatch rule, ELD configuration, or driver-training slide that applies 11/14/10 to a motorcoach is wrong on all three counts. Confirm this in the carrier's ELD configuration and driver handbook before relying on the summary above.

## 4. How the three clocks actually work (application rules)

1. **Common start point.** Both the 10-hour driving limit and the 15-hour on-duty limit run from the end of the same event: **8 consecutive hours off duty**. The 8 hours may consist of off duty, sleeper berth, or any combination of the two, and **there must be no on-duty or driving time during those 8 hours**. (FMCSA, *Interstate Passenger-Carrying Driver's Guide to Hours of Service*.)
2. **The 10-hour limit is cumulative driving time, not elapsed time.** The driver may drive in as many blocks as desired within the duty period; once cumulative driving reaches 10 hours, no further driving is permitted until another 8 consecutive hours off duty are taken.
3. **The 15-hour limit is a cap on driving, not on working.** After 15 hours on duty the driver **may continue non-driving work** but **may not drive**. The FMCSA guide is explicit: "You may do other work after being on duty 15 hours, but you may not drive."
4. **For passenger carriers the 15-hour clock counts on-duty time, so off-duty breaks extend it.** FMCSA guidance: "Off-duty time taken during the day, such as a lunch break or nap, does not count toward this 15-hour limit." FMCSA's own worked example: on duty at 06:00, work 7 hours, 1 hour off for lunch, work 8 more hours to 22:00 = 15 on-duty hours; no driving after 22:00. **This is a genuine difference from the property-carrier 14-hour window, which off-duty breaks do not extend.** Because this point is interpretive rather than plain regulatory text, confirm it against current § 395.5 and any FMCSA guidance in force on the date of use.
5. **Either limit ends driving independently.** Reaching 10 hours of driving bars further driving even at hour 11 of on-duty time; reaching 15 hours on duty bars further driving even with only 6 hours of driving used. Whichever comes first controls.
6. **Multiple-employer aggregation.** The limits apply "regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services" (§ 395.5(b)). Part-time, intermittent, and multiple-employer drivers must disclose prior on-duty time; FMCSA directs carriers to obtain a signed statement of total on-duty time for the preceding 7 days and the time the driver was last relieved from duty (§ 395.8(j)). Compensated work for a non-motor-carrier also counts as on-duty time (§ 395.2).

## 5. Worked examples

**Example A — driving limit bites first.** Driver has 8 consecutive hours off duty, comes on duty at 06:00. Drives 4 hours, takes 2 hours off duty, drives 6 hours (10 cumulative driving hours, clock at 18:00, 12 on-duty hours). **No further driving.** Driver may perform non-driving work until 15 on-duty hours are reached (21:00, with the 2-hour break excluded). Driving resumes only after 8 consecutive hours off duty.

**Example B — on-duty limit bites first.** Same 06:00 start. Driver is on duty 15 hours (with no off-duty break) at 21:00 but has driven only 7 hours. **No further driving after 21:00**, despite 3 unused driving hours. Driving resumes only after 8 consecutive hours off duty.

**Example C — weekly limit bites first.** Driver operates for a carrier that runs CMVs every day of the week and has accumulated 70 on-duty hours in the 8 consecutive days ending today. **No driving**, even with a fresh 8-hour break and zero driving today, until on-duty time in the rolling 8-day window drops below 70 hours.

## 6. Scope conditions under which these numbers are the answer

- **Interstate commerce.** § 390.3(a) is the hook for Part 395. If the operation is **intrastate only**, federal Part 395 does not govern; the state's own hours-of-service rules apply (many states adopt the federal 10/8/15 figures, several do not — verify the specific state's passenger-carrier rule).
- **No § 390.3(f) exemption.** The subchapter does not apply to, among others, **school bus operations** as defined in § 390.5 (§ 390.3(f)(1)) and **transportation performed by the Federal government, a State, or any political subdivision, or an agency established under an approved interstate compact** (§ 390.3(f)(2)) — e.g., many public transit authorities. Those operations fall outside § 395.5.
- **Non-business private motor carriers of passengers** are, per FMCSA guidance, **not subject to the recordkeeping requirements** of Part 395 (no record of duty status, no ELD) — but the driving-time limits themselves still apply; do not treat the logbook relief as an hours relief.
- **§ 395.1 exceptions are expressly preserved** ("Subject to the exceptions and exemptions in § 395.1"). Relevant ones for passenger operations:
  - **Sleeper berth, § 395.1(g)(3):** a driver of a passenger-carrying CMV with a sleeper berth conforming to § 393.76 may accumulate the equivalent of 8 consecutive hours off duty by taking two rest periods, if all four requirements of § 395.1(g)(3)(i)–(iv) are met.
  - **§ 395.1(e) short-haul relief:** FMCSA's passenger guide describes relief from the **record of duty status** requirement for drivers operating within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location and released within 14 consecutive hours. Treat this as a **paperwork** relief, not a driving-hours relief, and verify against the current § 395.1(e) text.
  - **Emergency relief (§ 395.1(c)):** §§ 395.3 and 395.5 do not apply to a carrier or driver providing direct assistance during a declared Federal, State, or local emergency, for the period of assistance or 5 days from the initial declaration, whichever is less.
- **No 34-hour restart in § 395.5.** Unlike § 395.3(c) for property carriers, § 395.5 contains no restart provision. A passenger driver who hits 60/70 hours becomes eligible to drive again only when the rolling 7- or 8-day on-duty total falls below the cap. Do not apply the property-carrier restart to a motorcoach driver without confirming a specific regulatory basis.
- **No 30-minute break requirement in § 395.5.** The § 395.3(a)(3)(ii) break requirement is written for property-carrying CMVs; § 395.5 contains no counterpart. Verify before relying on this in enforcement correspondence.
- **Adverse driving conditions:** § 395.1(b) provides limited additional driving time when a driver encounters adverse driving conditions. The exact mechanics and whether they reach a given passenger operation should be read from the current § 395.1(b) text before being applied — do not assume a 2-hour extension applies without checking.

## 7. Compliance checklist for the carrier

1. Classify the operation: passenger-carrying CMV? interstate? any § 390.3(f) exemption? — if intrastate or exempt, stop and apply the correct regime.
2. Configure the ELD/RODS engine to **10-hour driving / 8-consecutive-hour reset / 15-hour on-duty**, and to **60-in-7 or 70-in-8** as elected by the carrier's operating schedule — not to the property-carrier 11/14/10.
3. Elect and document the weekly schedule (60/7 if the carrier does not operate CMVs every day of the week; 70/8 if it does).
4. Train drivers that the 15-hour limit stops **driving**, not **working**, and that non-driving work remains permitted.
5. Train drivers and dispatchers that off-duty breaks extend the passenger 15-hour on-duty count but do not reset the 10-hour driving count.
6. Collect § 395.8(j) signed prior-duty statements from part-time/intermittent/multiple-employer drivers before use.
7. Retain the regulation citations (§ 395.5(a)(1), (a)(2), (b)) in the compliance file so each limit is traceable to text.

## 8. Verification of stated values

| Stated value | Where it appears | Consistent? |
|---|---|---|
| 10 hours driving | Ask 1 answer; § 395.5(a)(1); examples A and B | Yes — 10 ≤ 15 on-duty cap, so the driving limit never exceeds the duty limit |
| 8 consecutive hours off duty | Ask 2 answer; reset condition for both (a)(1) and (a)(2) | Yes — single reset event serves both daily limits |
| 15 hours on duty | Ask 3 answer; § 395.5(a)(2); examples A and B | Yes — 15 > 10, so the on-duty cap is the outer bound |
| 60 hours / 7 days; 70 hours / 8 days | Supplementary § 395.5(b) | Yes — labeled supplementary, cumulative, and additional; not offered as the answer to asks 1–3 |

No stated value contradicts any threshold stated elsewhere in this deliverable.

question: M4
answer:
ANSWER

In general industry, a US employer must protect an employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge from falling when that surface is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level. The trigger is inclusive: at exactly 4 feet, protection is required.

GOVERNING PROVISION

29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i) — Unprotected sides and edges: 'The employer must ensure that each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by one or more of the following: (A) Guardrail systems; (B) Safety net systems; or (C) Personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems.'

The identical 4-foot trigger appears in the residual paragraph, 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(15) — 'Walking-working surfaces not otherwise addressed': 'Except as provided elsewhere in this section or by other subparts of this part, the employer must ensure each employee on a walking-working surface 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by: (i) Guardrail systems; (ii) Safety net systems; or (iii) Personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems.'

So the answer is the same whether the surface is a named category or falls through to the catch-all.

HOW THE FOUR CONSTRAINTS ARE SATISFIED

1. General industry, not construction. The controlling text is 29 CFR Part 1910, Subpart D (Walking-Working Surfaces), specifically 1910.28. Construction's separate 6-foot trigger (29 CFR 1926.501(b)(1)) does not apply and is named here only to show the contrast; it is not the answer to this question. One cross-reference is unavoidable and should not be mistaken for a construction determination: 1910.28(b)(12)(i) directs that employees on scaffolds be protected in accordance with 29 CFR Part 1926, Subpart L, even in general industry.

2. Height above a lower level. 4 feet (1.2 m). Measured from the walking-working surface on which the employee stands, works or gains access, down to the lower level the employee could fall to.

3. US employer. 29 CFR 1910 is binding on employers in the United States under OSHA jurisdiction. Twenty-plus states and territories operate OSHA-approved State Plans; a State Plan may adopt a stricter trigger or stricter system criteria but may not be less effective than the federal standard. Where a State Plan applies, check its version of Subpart D before relying on the federal number.

4. Walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge. 1910.28(b)(1)(i) is the paragraph written for exactly this condition. 'Walking-working surface' means any horizontal or vertical surface on or through which an employee walks, works, or gains access to a work area or workplace location. 'Unprotected sides and edges' means any side or edge of a walking-working surface (except at entrances and other points of access) where there is no wall, guardrail system, or stair rail system to protect an employee from falling to a lower level.

WHAT THE 4-FOOT TRIGGER DOES AND DOES NOT DO

- Below 4 feet, 1910.28(b)(1)(i) does not require fall protection. Other duties can still attach below 4 feet: 1910.28(b)(6)(i) requires a guardrail system or travel restraint system for each employee less than 4 feet above dangerous equipment, unless the equipment is covered or guarded to eliminate the hazard.
- The 4-foot trigger is a height trigger. Several paragraphs of 1910.28 key off something other than height and must not be confused with it:
  - 1910.28(b)(13), low-slope roofs, keys off horizontal distance from the roof edge: less than 6 feet (1.6 m) from the edge — guardrail, safety net, travel restraint or personal fall arrest system; at least 6 feet but less than 15 feet — the same systems, or a designated area for work that is both infrequent and temporary; 15 feet (4.6 m) or more — those systems or a designated area, with no fall protection required if the work is both infrequent and temporary, plus a work rule prohibiting employees from going within 15 feet of the edge without fall protection. These are edge distances, not heights above a lower level.
  - 1910.28(b)(7), openings, keys off geometry: inside bottom edge of the opening less than 39 inches (99 cm) above the walking-working surface and outside bottom edge 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level.
  - 1910.28(b)(8) addresses repair, service and assembly pits less than 10 feet in depth; read the paragraph in full before treating a shallow pit as exempt.
- Other paragraphs that repeat the same 4-foot trigger for specific surfaces: 1910.28(b)(6)(ii) (4 feet or more above dangerous equipment), 1910.28(b)(11)(i) (unprotected side or edge of a stairway landing), 1910.28(b)(12)(ii) (rope descent systems), 1910.28(b)(14)(i) (slaughtering facility platforms).
- Means of protection, not the trigger, are set by 1910.28(b)(1)(i)(A)-(C) and by the system criteria in 1910.29 (guardrail, safety net, personal fall protection system design and performance). Those criteria are outside the scope of this height question.

COMPLIANCE PROCEDURE (apply directly)

Step 1 — Identify the walking-working surface and each side or edge of it that is not bounded by a wall, guardrail system, or stair rail system. Entrances and other points of access are excluded from 'unprotected side or edge.'

Step 2 — Establish the lower level for each such edge: the surface, equipment, or object an employee could fall to.

Step 3 — Measure vertically from the walking-working surface to that lower level at the edge.

Step 4 — Decision:
  - Height 4 feet (1.2 m) or more → fall protection is required under 1910.28(b)(1)(i) (or the applicable specific paragraph). Select at least one: guardrail system, safety net system, or personal fall protection system (personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning system). Where the employer can demonstrate that a required system is infeasible or creates a greater hazard, follow the fall protection plan route in 1910.28(b)(1) and 1910.29(k) rather than simply omitting protection.
  - Height under 4 feet → 1910.28(b)(1)(i) does not compel fall protection. Still screen for 1910.28(b)(6)(i) (dangerous equipment below 4 feet), 1910.28(b)(7) (openings), 1910.28(b)(8) (pits) and any other subpart of Part 1910 that imposes its own duty.

Worked example: a mezzanine deck 3 feet 10 inches above a concrete floor, open on one side with no rail. 1910.28(b)(1)(i) is not triggered (under 4 feet). Raise the deck to 4 feet 0 inches and the duty attaches — a guardrail, safety net, or personal fall protection system is required. If the floor below the open edge instead holds an energized conveyor or operating machinery, 1910.28(b)(6)(i) requires a guardrail system or travel restraint system even at the 3-foot-10-inch height.

SCOPE NOTE

This answer covers the federal general-industry baseline for the stated condition. It does not resolve State Plan variations, the system design criteria in 1910.29, training duties in 1910.30, or industry-specific subparts that may impose a different or additional duty.

question: M5
answer:
# Part 135 flight attendant rest after a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less

## Bottom line

| Ask | Answer | Authority |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Rest required after a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less | **At least 9 consecutive hours** | 14 CFR 135.273(b)(2) |
| 2. Minimum to which that rest may be reduced | **8 consecutive hours** — conditional, not automatic | 14 CFR 135.273(b)(3) |

## 1. Which rule governs

- **135.261(e):** 'Section 135.273 prescribes duty period limitations and rest requirements for flight attendants in all operations conducted under this part.' The flight-attendant duty/rest rule is therefore not keyed to scheduled vs. on-demand/charter status, and it is not displaced by the unscheduled-crew provisions of 135.267/135.269, which govern flight crewmembers. For a Part 135 on-demand charter operator that uses flight attendants, 135.273 is the governing rule.
- **135.273(a) definitions that control the arithmetic:**
  - *Flight attendant*: an individual, other than a flight crewmember, assigned by the certificate holder in accordance with the required minimum crew complement under its operations specifications, or in addition to that minimum, to duty in an aircraft during flight time, whose duties include cabin-safety responsibilities.
  - *Rest period*: 'the period free of all responsibility for work or duty should the occasion arise.' This is the operative constraint — a rest period is not merely non-flight time; reserve, standby, on-call, administrative duty, or any company-imposed obligation that could be worked defeats it.
  - *Duty period*: elapsed time from reporting for an assignment involving flight time to release from that assignment by the certificate holder, computed in UTC or local time.

## 2. Ask 1 — the full rest requirement: 9 consecutive hours

135.273(b)(1) sets the ceiling on the assignment: no certificate holder may assign a flight attendant to a scheduled duty period of more than 14 hours, except as allowed by (b)(4) through (b)(6). For the case in the question — a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less — 135.273(b)(2) sets the rest:

> (b)(2) 'Except as provided in paragraph (b)(3) of this section, a flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less as provided under paragraph (b)(1) of this section must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 9 consecutive hours. This rest period must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.'

**Answer 1 = 9 consecutive hours.** Four attributes make a rest period compliant, and a scheduling system must test all four:

1. **Consecutive** — 9 uninterrupted clock hours; it may not be assembled from fragments or split around a deadhead, a reposition, or a phone call.
2. **At least 9 hours** — 9:00 is the floor for the scheduled case; there is no rounding down.
3. **Correctly positioned** — the rest must run from completion (release) of the scheduled duty period to commencement (report) of the subsequent duty period. Rest that overlaps the prior duty period does not count.
4. **Free of all responsibility for work or duty** — per the (a) definition, no reserve/standby status, no on-call, no assigned office or training duty, no requirement to remain reachable in a way that constitutes a duty obligation.

## 3. Ask 2 — the reduction floor: 8 consecutive hours, with three conditions

> (b)(3) 'The rest period required under paragraph (b)(2) of this section may be scheduled or reduced to 8 consecutive hours if the flight attendant is provided a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours; this subsequent rest period must be scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period and must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.'

**Answer 2 = 8 consecutive hours**, and only if all three conditions are satisfied:

1. **Compensatory rest of at least 10 consecutive hours** is in fact provided (not merely planned);
2. that compensatory rest is **scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period** (the trigger clock starts at the *start* of the 8-hour reduced rest, not at its end and not at the end of the following duty period); and
3. that compensatory rest **falls between completion of the scheduled duty period and commencement of the subsequent duty period**.

**8 hours is the absolute floor.** No provision of 135.273 authorizes less than 8 consecutive hours following a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less.

Two reinforcing provisions apply to both answers:

- **135.273(b)(10):** no certificate holder may assign a flight attendant any duty period unless the flight attendant has had at least the minimum rest required under the section.
- **135.273(b)(11):** no certificate holder may assign a flight attendant to perform any duty during a required rest period.

## 4. Do not substitute the extended-duty numbers

The rule contains a second, higher rest regime for the longer scheduled duty periods authorized by (b)(4) through (b)(6). Those numbers are **not** the answer here:

| Scenario | Rest | May be reduced to | Compensatory rest | Additional cap |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Scheduled duty period **14 hours or less** — (b)(2)/(b)(3) | **9 consecutive hours** | **8 consecutive hours** | at least 10 consecutive hours, beginning within 24 hours of the start of the reduced rest | — |
| Duty period longer than 14 hours under (b)(4)-(b)(6) — (b)(7)/(b)(8)/(b)(9) | per (b)(7) | 10 consecutive hours | at least 14 consecutive hours, beginning within 24 hours of the start of the reduced rest | (b)(9): no duty period of more than 14 hours during the 24-hour period commencing after the beginning of the reduced rest |

The 10-hour reduction and the 14-hour compensatory rest quoted from (b)(8) belong exclusively to the over-14-hour regime. Applying them to a 14-hour-or-less duty period, or applying the 8-hour floor to an extended-duty assignment, is an error in either direction.

## 5. Assumptions on which these figures rest

- The individual meets the 135.273(a) definition of flight attendant — i.e., is assigned under the certificate holder's operations specifications minimum crew complement or in addition to it. The obligation to carry a flight attendant in the first place typically arises from 135.107 (aircraft seating more than 19 passengers) or from the operations specifications; if the individual is not a 'flight attendant' as defined, 135.273 does not apply to that person and these figures do not govern.
- The certificate holder has **not** elected the alternative in 135.273(c) (see §7 below).
- These are the **regulatory minimums**. A collective bargaining agreement, a company manual, or a customer/contract standard may be stricter and would control as a matter of contract even though it exceeds the FAA floor.
- The question is read as asking about the **scheduled** duty period, which is the unit the rule uses.

## 6. Implementation procedure

1. **Classify the assignment.** Determine the *scheduled* duty period length for the flight attendant's assignment. If ≤14 hours, apply the 9/8 rule. If the schedule exceeds 14 hours, the assignment must be justified under (b)(4)-(b)(6) and the (b)(7)/(b)(8)/(b)(9) rest regime applies instead — stop and route to that rule.
2. **Default to 9 hours.** Build the pairing with ≥9:00 consecutive hours from release to next report. This is the baseline; the 8-hour version is an exception that must be affirmatively elected and documented.
3. **Elect 8 hours only with the compensatory rest locked in.** Before publishing the schedule, place a ≥10:00 consecutive rest period that begins no later than 24 hours after the start of the reduced rest and that sits between the two duty periods.
4. **Validate the rest is genuine rest.** Screen the 9- or 8-hour window for reserve, standby, on-call, training, positioning as a duty assignment, and any other responsibility for work — any of these voids the rest under the (a) definition and triggers (b)(10)/(b)(11).
5. **Record the basis.** Capture which paragraph authorized the rest (9-hour standard vs. 8-hour reduced), the release and report times that establish the rest window, and the start/end of the compensatory rest.

Reference validation logic (illustrative, to be implemented in the crew-tracking/scheduling system):

```
validateRest(prevDuty, nextDuty, records):
    restStart  = prevDuty.release            # actual release time
    restEnd    = nextDuty.report             # actual report time
    restHours  = hoursBetween(restStart, restEnd)
    sched      = prevDuty.scheduledDutyHours # from the published schedule, not actual

    if sched <= 14:                          # 135.273(b)(1),(b)(2),(b)(3)
        if restHours >= 9:  return OK_9HR
        if restHours >= 8 and compensatoryOK(restStart, records, required=10):
            return OK_8HR_REDUCED
        return VIOLATION_135_273_b_2
    else:                                    # 135.273(b)(4)-(b)(9)
        return validateExtendedDutyRest(prevDuty, nextDuty, records)

compensatoryOK(reducedRestStart, records, required):
    c = records.subsequentRestPeriodAfter(reducedRestStart)
    return c.durationHours >= required
       and c.start <= addHours(reducedRestStart, 24)   # must BEGIN within 24h
       and c.start >= reducedRestStart
       and c.occursBetween(completedDutyPeriod, subsequentDutyPeriod)
```

## 7. The one alternative that would change the numbers

135.273(c) lets a certificate holder apply the **flight crewmember** flight time and duty limitations and rest requirements of Part 135 to flight attendants for all its operations, but only if it establishes written procedures covering all flight attendants in the operation, includes the subpart F flight crewmember requirements as appropriate (except that on-board rest facilities are not required), adds one flight attendant to the minimum complement for each flight crewmember above the type-certificate minimum, and has those procedures **approved by the Administrator and described or referenced in its operations specifications**. Under such an approved election the rest figures come from 135.265/135.267/135.269 rather than from 135.273(b)(2)/(b)(3) — for example, 135.265(b) scales scheduled rest to scheduled flight time (9, 10, or 11 consecutive hours) with the 135.265(c) reductions to 8, 8, or 9 hours against 10-, 11-, and 12-hour compensatory rests. Absent that approved election and ops-spec reference, the 9-hour / 8-hour answer above is the operative requirement.

## 8. Records, enforcement, and the scheduled-vs-actual question

- **Records.** Maintain the duty and rest records the certificate holder is required to keep (see 135.63), showing report and release times, the scheduled duty period length used to select the rule, which paragraph authorized the rest (9-hour standard or 8-hour reduced), and the start and end of any compensatory rest. The reduced-rest election must be documented *when the schedule is built*, not reconstructed afterward.
- **Enforcement exposure.** If the 8-hour reduced rest is used and the 10-hour compensatory rest is not in fact given within the 24-hour trigger, the original assignment was never authorized by (b)(3), and the flight attendant was assigned duty without the minimum rest required by (b)(2) — a violation of (b)(3) together with (b)(10). Assigning any duty inside a required rest period is a separate violation of (b)(11).
- **Scheduled vs. actual.** The rule is written in terms of the *scheduled* duty period, and the answer above is expressed that way. If actual operations run the duty period past the scheduled length, the rest that was owed is still the rest required for the scheduled assignment, but the certificate holder should re-evaluate the pairing against (b)(1) and, if the duty period is being extended beyond 14 hours as a matter of schedule, against (b)(4)-(b)(6) with the corresponding (b)(7)/(b)(8) rest — in coordination with its principal operations inspector and any ops-spec conditions.

question: M6
answer:
ANSWER

A helicopter beginning a VFR flight in the United States must carry, beyond the fuel needed to reach the first point of intended landing, at least 20 minutes of fuel at normal cruising speed. This is the legal minimum under both the general operating rules and the commercial helicopter VFR rule. There is no separate day/night helicopter VFR reserve: it is 20 minutes day or night.

REGULATORY BASIS

1. Part 91 general operating rules — 14 CFR §91.151(b): 'No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes.'

2. Part 135 commercial helicopter VFR — 14 CFR §135.209(b): 'No person may begin a flight operation in a helicopter under VFR unless, considering wind and forecast weather conditions, it has enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising fuel consumption, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes.'

3. The 30-minute day and 45-minute night figures in §91.151(a) and §135.209(a) apply to airplanes, not helicopters. They do not increase the helicopter reserve at night.

HOW TO APPLY THE REQUIREMENT

Step 1. Compute the fuel required to fly to the first point of intended landing, considering wind and forecast weather conditions.

Step 2. Add 20 minutes of fuel at normal cruising speed or normal cruising fuel consumption, as applicable. Use usable fuel; unusable fuel does not count toward the reserve.

Step 3. Ensure total usable fuel at takeoff is at least: fuel to first point of intended landing + 20-minute reserve + any taxi, startup, hover, and contingency fuel the operator elects to plan. The regulatory VFR reserve itself is the 20-minute increment after the first landing point; taxi and contingency fuel are separate planning allowances.

Step 4. Do not plan to consume the reserve. It is a minimum that must remain after reaching the first point of intended landing.

CONVERSION TO FUEL QUANTITY

Reserve fuel in gallons = normal cruise burn rate in gallons/hour × (20/60) = burn rate ÷ 3.

Reserve fuel in pounds = normal cruise burn rate in pounds/hour × (20/60) = burn rate ÷ 3.

Reserve fuel in liters = normal cruise burn rate in liters/hour × (20/60) = burn rate ÷ 3.

Examples using the 20-minute requirement:
- 15 gal/h normal cruise burn → 15 ÷ 3 = 5 gal reserve.
- 180 lb/h normal cruise burn → 180 ÷ 3 = 60 lb reserve.
- 90 L/h normal cruise burn → 90 ÷ 3 = 30 L reserve.

Use the helicopter's actual normal-cruise usable fuel burn. Hover, taxi, and climb burn are typically higher and should be accounted for separately in the trip fuel and planning allowances.

OPERATING-RULE NOTE

Under Part 91 the answer is 20 minutes. Under Part 135 helicopter VFR the answer is also 20 minutes. The answer therefore does not change merely because the flight is commercial helicopter VFR rather than private Part 91. An operator or company may impose a higher minimum; the regulatory minimum remains 20 minutes. If the flight is conducted IFR, a different fuel rule applies and is outside this VFR question.

The current specification of HTTP/2 is RFC 9113, "HTTP/2", Standards Track (Proposed Standard), published June 2022, edited by Martin Thomson (Mozilla) and Cory Benfield (Apple Inc.), ISSN 2070-1721. It is the base HTTP/2 specification and the newest document in the RFC Editor's HTTP/2 subject area.

2. RFC 9113 obsoletes exactly two RFCs:

(RFC 7230, the HTTP/1.1 message syntax at the time, was separately obsoleted by RFC 9112, "HTTP/1.1" — an unrelated HTTP/1.1 revision, not by RFC 9113.)

ANSWER

1) The RFC that formally deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 is RFC 8996, "Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1" (IETF, March 2021; part of BCP 195). Authors: K. Moriarty and S. Farrell.

2) It gave the RFCs that defined those protocol versions the status Historic: both RFC 2246 (TLS 1.0) and RFC 4346 (TLS 1.1) "have been moved to Historic status."

VERBATIM SUPPORT (rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996, Abstract):
  "This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those documents have been moved to Historic status."

Section 1 (Introduction) repeats the action and adds the reason:
  "Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 [RFC2246] and 1.1 [RFC4346] were superseded by TLS 1.2 [RFC5246] in 2008, which has now itself been superseded by TLS 1.3 [RFC8446]. ... Therefore, it is timely to further deprecate TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and DTLS 1.0. Accordingly, the aforementioned documents have been moved to Historic status."

PER-DOCUMENT DISPOSITION (all three named in the abstract/introduction):
  - RFC 2246 (TLS 1.0)  -> Historic
  - RFC 4346 (TLS 1.1)  -> Historic
  - RFC 4347 (DTLS 1.0) -> Historic (deprecated by the same document; DTLS 1.2 / RFC 6347 is explicitly NOT deprecated, and there is no DTLS 1.1)
  Additionally, RFC 5469 (DES/IDEA cipher suites) was moved to Historic as a consequence, since the only TLS versions for which those suites were defined are now Historic.

TERMINOLOGY NOTE (relevant because the question uses "deprecated" loosely):
  - "Deprecated" in RFC 8996 is the protocol-level statement: the versions must no longer be used.
  - "Moved to Historic" is the document-level status change recorded by the RFC Editor for RFC 2246, RFC 4346, RFC 4347, and RFC 5469.
  - "Superseded/obsoleted" is a different relation: RFC 5246 obsoleted RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 as protocol specifications in 2008, and RFC 8446 obsoleted RFC 5246 in 2018. RFC 8996 does not itself obsolete RFC 2246 or RFC 4346; it deprecates the protocols and moves the documents to Historic, and it Updates a long list of RFCs that normatively reference TLS 1.0/1.1 (plus RFC 7525, which is why it is part of BCP 195).

DOCUMENT STATUS OF RFC 8996 ITSELF: "This memo documents an Internet Best Current Practice" (BCP 195), not a Standards Track document.

OUT OF SCOPE BUT WORTH ONE LINE: TLS 1.2's defining RFC 5246 was not moved to Historic by RFC 8996; it had already been obsoleted by RFC 8446 (TLS 1.3).

SOURCES: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996 ; https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8996/ ; https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc8996/history/ (RFC 8996 published 2021-03-23).

# UK National Minimum Wage / National Living Wage — rates applying from 1 April 2026

## 1. Headline answers

| # | Question | Rate from 1 April 2026 | Previous rate (to 31 Mar 2026) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | National Living Wage — workers aged 21 and over | **£12.71 per hour** | £12.21 | +£0.50 (+4.1%) |
| 2 | National Minimum Wage — 18 to 20 year old rate | **£10.85 per hour** | £10.00 | +£0.85 (+8.5%) |

Both are the statutory rates in force from **1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027**, to the penny, UK-wide (England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland).

## 2. Statutory basis (primary source)

**The National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026, S.I. 2026/357** — made 19 March 2026, coming into force 1 April 2026, extending to England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland. Signed by Kate Dearden, Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State, Department for Business and Trade.

- Regulation 2(2): in regulation 4 of the National Minimum Wage Regulations 2015 (S.I. 2015/621) — the national living wage — for `£12.21` substitute `£12.71`.
- Regulation 2(3)(a): in regulation 4A(1)(b) — workers aged 18 or over but not yet 21 — for `£10.00` substitute `£10.85`.
- The Explanatory Note states in words: NLW for workers aged 21 or over increases from £12.21 to £12.71 per hour; the rate for workers aged 18 or over (but not yet 21) increases from £10.00 to £10.85 per hour.

Independent corroboration, all agreeing with the SI:
- Low Pay Commission, *Minimum wage rates for 2026* (published 26 November 2025): Government announced the 2026 increases and **accepted the LPC recommendations in full**; NLW 21+ £12.71 (+50p, 4.1%); 18-20 rate £10.85 (+85p, 8.5%).
- Low Pay Commission, *The National Minimum Wage in 2026* (published 1 April 2026): same table, "NMW rates to apply from 1 April 2026".
- GOV.UK, *National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage rates*: April 2026 row — 21 and over £12.71; 18 to 20 £10.85; under 18 £8; apprentice £8.

## 3. Full April 2026 rate card (load all rows into payroll, apply per worker age band)

| Band | From 1 Apr 2026 | 1 Apr 2025 – 31 Mar 2026 | Change | Change % |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **National Living Wage (21 and over)** | **£12.71** | £12.21 | +£0.50 | 4.1% |
| **18–20 Year Old Rate** | **£10.85** | £10.00 | +£0.85 | 8.5% |
| 16–17 Year Old Rate | £8.00 | £7.55 | +£0.45 | 6.0% |
| Apprentice Rate | £8.00 | £7.55 | +£0.45 | 6.0% |
| Accommodation offset (per day, not an hourly rate) | £11.10 | £10.66 | +£0.44 | 4.1% |

Only the first two rows are the subject of the request. The others are shown so the correct row is selected and the adjacent bands are not picked up in error — in particular, £8.00 is the 16-17/apprentice rate and must not be applied to an 18-20 year old, and £11.10 is a daily accommodation offset, not an hourly rate.

## 4. Payroll application notes

**Effective date.** Apply from 1 April 2026. New rates bite from the first pay reference period beginning on or after 1 April 2026. Where a pay reference period straddles 31 March / 1 April 2026, compliance is measured on average hourly pay across the whole period, so the safe operational approach is to apply the new rate to the entire straddling period rather than splitting it — splitting risks a shortfall in that period.

**Age banding.** NLW applies to workers aged 21 and over; workers aged 20 and under remain on the NMW age rates (18-20 = £10.85; under 18 = £8.00). A worker reaching 21 moves from the 18-20 rate to £12.71, and a worker reaching 18 moves from £8.00 to £10.85. Note: the precise mid-period age-transition rule sits in regulation 4A of S.I. 2015/621 as amended, which is not in the retrieved passages — confirm the transition rule against the 2015 Regulations before coding an automatic birthday uplift, and in the interim flag such workers manually at the payroll cut-off.

**Apprentices.** The £8.00 apprentice rate applies to apprentices aged under 19, and to those aged 19 or over in the first year of their apprenticeship. An apprentice aged 21 who has completed the first year of the apprenticeship is entitled to £12.71, not £8.00.

**Accommodation offset.** The maximum offset for living accommodation provided by the employer is £11.10 per day (£77.70 for a 7-day week). This is a separate limit; it does not change the hourly rates and cannot be used to take pay below the applicable hourly rate.

**Do not load the April 2027 rates.** GOV.UK also publishes an April 2027 row (21+ £13.21; 18-20 £11.27; under 18 £8.31; apprentice £8.31). Those take effect 1 April 2027 and must not be used for 2026/27. Keep them in a separate, inactive rate table.

**Rounding.** Rates are set to the nearest penny; never round an hourly rate down. Where hours × rate produces a fraction of a penny, round the resulting pay **up**:
- 37.5-hour week, 21+: 37.5 × £12.71 = £476.625 → pay at least **£476.63** per week.
- 37.5-hour week, 18–20: 37.5 × £10.85 = £406.875 → pay at least **£406.88** per week.
- Annualised at 1,950 hours (37.5 × 52): 21+ £24,784.50; 18–20 £21,157.50.

**What reduces NMW pay.** Pay for NMW purposes is gross pay before tax/NIC but after deductions that benefit the employer (uniform, tools, travel between assignments) and after salary sacrifice (pension, cycle-to-work, car schemes). Check any salary-sacrificed population against £12.71 / £10.85 for the 2026/27 year, not against the old rates.

**Records.** Retain National Minimum Wage records for 6 years (HMRC enforcement window).

## 5. Not the same thing as

- **The Living Wage Foundation 'real Living Wage'** — a separate, voluntary rate set by the LWF, not a statutory rate. The statutory National Living Wage from April 2026 is £12.71.
- **Any regional variant** — there is none; NMW/NLW is set UK-wide by Westminster and the 2026 Regulations extend to England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.
- **The April 2027 figures** — £13.21 / £11.27, effective 1 April 2027.

## 6. Source check and status

Sources checked **23 November 2026**: legislation.gov.uk (S.I. 2026/357, made version, and the draft affirmative instrument laid before Parliament) and GOV.UK (LPC *Minimum wage rates for 2026*, LPC *The National Minimum Wage in 2026*, and the NMW rates guidance page). The Regulations were made on 19 March 2026 and in force on 1 April 2026, so at the check date these are **enacted, in-force figures — not projections or autumn-announcement estimates**. All sources agree; no source in the retrieved material gives a conflicting 2026 figure.

Nothing in this request was blocked: both requested figures are confirmed by the operative statutory instrument and by two independent official publications.

answer:
US Social Security contribution and benefit base (OASDI taxable maximum) for tax year 2026

ANSWER

$184,500.

For 2026, the maximum amount of earnings subject to the Social Security (OASDI) payroll tax is $184,500. This is the official figure — it was announced by the Social Security Administration in the fall of 2025 as part of the 2026 automatic adjustments and has been published in final form; it is not an estimate or projection.

SCOPE / DEFINITION

- 'Contribution and benefit base' is the statutory term (Social Security Act) for the annual OASDI earnings limit. The same limit applies both to earnings subject to the OASDI tax and to earnings counted in a benefit computation — hence 'contribution and benefit base.' It is commonly called the 'taxable maximum' or 'Social Security wage base.'
- The base applies only to OASDI (Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance). Medicare Hospital Insurance (HI) has had no earnings cap since 1993, so the answer to 'the most earnings subject to the Social Security payroll tax' is the OASDI base, $184,500. Medicare tax continues on all covered wages above that amount, plus the 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax on wages over $200,000 (employer withholding threshold).
- Self-employment (SECA): the same $184,500 base applies to the OASDI portion of net self-employment income, taxed at 12.4%.

SOURCE VERIFICATION (four independent official confirmations, all in agreement)

1. SSA, Contribution and Benefit Base (ssa.gov/oact/COLA/cbb.html): the annual table lists 2026 = $184,500 (2025 = $176,100; 2027 = $192,300).
2. SSA, Detailed Calculator update page (ssa.gov/oact/anypia/update.html): 'Contribution and benefit base for 2026: $184,500'; also gives the 'old-law' base for 2026 = $137,100 and the 2024 national average wage index = $69,846.57.
3. SSA, Fast Facts & Figures About Social Security, 2026: 'Maximum earnings subject to Social Security taxes, 2026 — OASDI 184,500; HI No limit.'
4. IRS Publication 15 (Circular E), Employer's Tax Guide, 2026 revision (dated Dec 15, 2025): 'The social security wage base limit is $184,500.' IRS Topic No. 751 repeats the same figure.

STATUTORY DERIVATION (confirms, rather than replaces, the published figure)

Under the automatic-adjustment formula, the base for year Y = $60,600 (the 1994 base) × (national average wage index for Y-2 ÷ NAWI for 1992), rounded to the nearest multiple of $300, and never reduced below the prior year's base. For 2026, Y-2 = 2024, NAWI 2024 = $69,846.57, NAWI 1992 = $22,935.42:

  $60,600 × $69,846.57 ÷ $22,935.42 = $184,548.70 (approx.)
  $184,548.70 ÷ $300 = 615.16 → 615 × $300 = $184,500

So the formula independently reproduces $184,500. (The same page's 2027 determination, $192,300, uses NAWI 2025 = $72,800.33: $60,600 × 72,800.33 ÷ 22,935.42 = $192,353.14 → $192,300. Note that $192,300 is the 2027 figure and is not the answer to a 2026 question.)

PAYROLL CONSEQUENCES AT THE $184,500 BASE (for the 2026 tax year)

| Item | Rate | Maximum amount |
|---|---|---|
| OASDI — employee | 6.2% | $11,439.00 |
| OASDI — employer | 6.2% | $11,439.00 |
| OASDI — employee + employer (FICA) | 12.4% | $22,878.00 |
| OASDI — self-employed (SECA) | 12.4% | $22,878.00 |
| Medicare (HI) — employee and employer, each | 1.45% | No limit |
| Additional Medicare Tax — employee only | 0.9% | No limit; applies to wages over $200,000 (withholding threshold; filing-status thresholds apply on the return) |

Arithmetic check against the published data: $184,500 × 6.2% = $11,439.00; × 2 = $22,878.00; × 12.4% = $22,878.00. SSA Fast Facts 2026 reports the self-employed maximum as OASI $19,557 + DI $3,321 = $22,878, which reconciles exactly with the base and rate above. No derived figure exceeds the $184,500 base.

CROSS-YEAR REFERENCE (for context only; not the answer)

1991 $53,400 … 2020 $137,700; 2021 $142,800; 2022 $147,000; 2023 $160,200; 2024 $168,600; 2025 $176,100; 2026 $184,500; 2027 $192,300.

OTHER 2026 THRESHOLDS THAT ARE OFTEN CONFUSED WITH THE BASE (distinct figures, not the answer)

- 'Old-law' contribution and benefit base, 2026: $137,100 (used for certain benefit computations under the pre-1977 law; not a payroll-tax cap).
- Domestic/household workers: Social Security and Medicare taxes apply if cash wages of $3,000 or more are paid in 2026.
- Election workers: $2,500 or more in cash or equivalent compensation in 2026.
- One work credit (quarter of coverage) in 2026: $1,890; four credits require $7,560.

CAVEATS

- The figure is for calendar/tax year 2026 and is fixed by statute for that year; it is not affected by an individual's filing status, age, or earnings pattern.
- Railroad workers covered under the Railroad Retirement Act use a separate but identically sized tier structure administered by the RRB; the OASDI-equivalent taxable maximum for 2026 is likewise $184,500, but payroll reporting runs through the RRB, not Form 941/W-2 Social Security boxes.
- Amounts above the base remain subject to Medicare HI tax (1.45% each) and to the Additional Medicare Tax where applicable; they are also not credited toward Social Security benefits.

answer:
# FMCSA Short-Haul (RODS) Exception — Radius and Release-Hour Limits

## 1. Direct answers

| # | Question | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Radius of the normal work reporting location within which the driver must operate | **150 air miles** (172.6 statute miles) |
| 2 | Consecutive hours within which the driver must be released from work | **14 consecutive hours** |

Authority: 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1) — the '150 air-mile radius driver' short-haul exception. Jurisdiction: US federal (FMCSA), interstate/foreign commerce. The exemption relieves the driver of the records-of-duty-status requirement (49 CFR 395.8) and the supporting-documents requirement (49 CFR 395.11).

## 2. Governing text

49 CFR 395.1(e)(1) — a driver is exempt from 395.8 and 395.11 if all of the following hold:

- **(i) Radius.** 'The driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location.'
- **(ii) Release.** 'The driver, except a driver-salesperson, returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours.'
- **(iii) Off-duty period.** (A) A property-carrying CMV driver has at least 10 consecutive hours off duty separating each 14 hours on duty; (B) a passenger-carrying CMV driver has at least 8 consecutive hours off duty separating each 14 hours on duty.
- **(iv) Time records.** The employing motor carrier maintains and retains for 6 months accurate and true time records showing: (A) the time the driver reports for duty each day; (B) total hours on duty each day; (C) the time the driver is released from duty each day; (D) the total time for the preceding 7 days per 395.8(j)(2) for drivers used for the first time or intermittently.

## 3. How each figure is measured (the part that decides pass/fail)

**Radius — air miles, not road miles.**
- 'Air miles' means straight-line (great-circle) distance between the normal work reporting location and the point in question. 150 air miles = 172.6 statute miles. These are the same threshold expressed in two units — do not treat 172.6 as a separate or additional limit.
- The boundary is measured from the *normal work reporting location* (the fixed location where the driver reports to and is released from work), not from the driver's residence, the terminal generally, or the day's first stop.
- The test is operational: every point the driver reaches during the tour must lie inside the 150 air-mile circle. Because the boundary is straight-line, a road route substantially longer than 150 miles can still qualify; conversely, a 140-road-mile trip around an obstruction can exceed 150 air miles. Verify with straight-line distance, and dispatch with a margin for GPS variance and rerouting rather than planning to the exact boundary.

**Release clock — 14 consecutive hours from coming on duty to release at the reporting location.**
- The clock starts when the driver reports for duty / comes on duty and stops only when the driver is *both* (a) back at the normal work reporting location *and* (b) released from work. Returning inside 14 hours but being held on duty past the 14th hour fails the condition.
- It is elapsed consecutive clock time. Off-duty time taken during the tour does not pause or extend it (same structural feature as the 395.3(a)(2) 14-hour window).
- Worked checks: report 06:00, released 19:45 → 13 h 45 m, qualifies. Report 06:00, released 20:15 → 14 h 15 m, does not qualify; the driver must keep RODS for that tour.
- The 14-hour release limit is not the 11-hour driving limit, not the 14-hour driving window of 395.3(a)(2), and not the 60/70-hour limit; those continue to apply on their own terms. The (e)(1) exemption is from 395.8 and 395.11 only.

**Driver-salesperson carve-out.** The return-and-release-within-14-hours condition in (e)(1)(ii) does not apply to a driver-salesperson (as defined in 395.2). All other (e)(1) conditions — radius, off-duty period, time records — still apply. For every other driver the 14-hour answer is unconditional.

**Property vs passenger.** Both classes use the same 150 air miles and the same 14 consecutive hours. The only difference in (e)(1) is the required off-duty period separating each 14 hours on duty: 10 consecutive hours for property-carrying, 8 consecutive hours for passenger-carrying. Neither difference changes the answers to asks 1 and 2.

## 4. Provisions that are often mistaken for this one (do not substitute their numbers)

| Provision | Radius | Hour figure | What it is |
|---|---|---|---|
| **395.1(e)(1)** — 150 air-mile radius driver | **150 air miles** | **released within 14 consecutive hours** | The short-haul RODS/ELD-supporting-document exception. This is the answer. |
| 395.1(e)(2) — property-carrying CMV not requiring a CDL | 150 air miles | return at end of each duty tour; no driving after the 14th hour on 5 days of any 7, and after the 16th hour on 2 days of any 7 | Separate exemption from 395.3(a)(2), 395.8, 395.11; drivers using it are ineligible for (e)(1), (g) and (o). The 16-hour allowance here is a two-days-per-week driving limit, not the release deadline for the general short-haul exception. |
| 395.1(o) — 16-hour exception | n/a | released within 16 hours after coming on duty following 10 consecutive hours off duty; return to reporting location for the previous 5 duty tours; not used in the previous 6 consecutive days | A driving-window extension, not a RODS exemption. |
| 395.1(p) — motion picture production sites | **100 air miles** | separate daily driving limits follow | The only place the 100 air-mile figure appears in current Part 395 short-haul-adjacent text. It does not apply to general short-haul operations. |

Note on the '100 air-mile' label: some FMCSA ELD FAQ answers still use the phrase '100 air-mile radius (short-haul) exception'. That is legacy terminology from pre-2013 rule text; the current in-force short-haul radius in 395.1(e)(1) is 150 air miles. The same FAQ pages correctly state the operative test as 150 air miles with release within 14 hours, including for Canada/Mexico-domiciled drivers entering the US.

## 5. Compliance verification procedure

For each driver claimed under 395.1(e)(1), the carrier should be able to evidence all of the following on audit:

1. **Designated normal work reporting location** recorded for the driver (one fixed address per driver assignment).
2. **Radius test:** straight-line distance from that location to the farthest point served on the tour is ≤ 150 air miles. Keep the distance calculation or the geocoded route map with the driver's file.
3. **Release test:** daily time record shows report-for-duty time and release-from-duty time, with the interval ≤ 14 hours 00 minutes, and shows release occurring at the normal work reporting location.
4. **Off-duty test:** ≥ 10 consecutive hours off duty between tours for property-carrying drivers, ≥ 8 for passenger-carrying drivers.
5. **Records retention:** the above time records retained 6 months; for drivers used for the first time or intermittently, the preceding 7 days' total time per 395.8(j)(2) also retained.
6. **Failure handling:** any tour breaching 150 air miles or 14 consecutive hours is outside the exception — the driver must complete RODS (paper or ELD) for that tour. A pattern of breaches means the driver should not be managed as short-haul at all.

## 6. Caveats and verification notes

- The figures above are taken from the current eCFR text of 49 CFR 395.1 and the 2024 printed CFR volume, both of which read 150 air miles and 14 consecutive hours. Confirm against the in-force 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1) at the time of use, since notice-and-comment rulemaking can change either figure.
- State intrastate hours-of-service rules may set different radii or hour limits for drivers not in interstate commerce; this answer covers the federal FMCSA rule only.
- The exemption is conditional on all four (e)(1) elements. A driver who satisfies the radius and the 14-hour release but lacks the required off-duty period or the carrier's time records is not exempt.

answer:
ANSWER

For tax year 2026, the limit on an employee's elective deferrals to a 401(k) plan, before any catch-up contribution, is $24,500.

This is the IRC §402(g)(1) limit on the exclusion for elective deferrals. It is an individual (not a plan) limit, and it is also capped at 100% of the employee's compensation — the operative rule is the lesser of $24,500 or 100% of compensation. For any employee earning at least $24,500 in 2026, the binding number is $24,500.

AUTHORITY

- IRS Notice 2025-67, '2026 Amounts Relating to Retirement Plans and IRAs, as Adjusted for Changes in Cost-of-Living': 'The limitation under section 402(g)(1) on the exclusion for elective deferrals described in section 402(g)(3), which includes elective deferrals made to the Thrift Savings Plan, is increased from $23,500 to $24,500.'
- IRS, 'COLA increases for dollar limitations on benefits and contributions' (2026 cost-of-living adjustments, IR-2025-111), table '401(k), 403(b), profit-sharing plans, etc.': Elective deferrals — 2026: $24,500 (2025: $23,500; 2024: $23,000; 2023: $22,500).
- IRS, 'Retirement Topics — Contributions': 'The basic limit on elective deferrals is $24,500 in 2026, $23,500 in 2025 ... or 100% of the employee's compensation, whichever is less.'

Both the statutory notice and the IRS limits table agree, so the figure is not a projection or an indexation estimate — it is the published 2026 amount.

WHAT THE $24,500 COVERS

- Applies to employee elective deferrals under a 401(k) plan: pre-tax salary reduction deferrals and designated Roth elective deferrals alike. Roth and traditional deferrals share this one limit; designating deferrals as Roth does not create additional room.
- Automatic-enrollment contributions count as elective deferrals and consume the same $24,500.
- The limit is applied per individual per calendar year, not per plan. An employee who participates in more than one 401(k) plan (or a 401(k) plus a 403(b), SARSEP, or SIMPLE IRA) during 2026 must aggregate all elective deferrals across those plans against the single $24,500 figure. Deferring $24,500 into each of two plans is an excess deferral.
- Employer contributions — matching and nonelective — do not count against §402(g). They are tested against the separate §415(c) annual-additions limit ($72,000 for 2026).

WHAT IT EXCLUDES (context only — not part of the answer)

- Catch-up contributions under §414(v) are outside this figure. For 2026 the age-50-and-over catch-up limit is $8,000 (up from $7,500), and the SECURE 2.0 enhanced catch-up for participants who attain age 60, 61, 62, or 63 in 2026 remains $11,250. A participant aged 50+ therefore has a total deferral capacity of $32,500 ($24,500 + $8,000) if the plan permits catch-ups.
- SIMPLE 401(k) plans are subject to a different deferral limit ($17,000 for 2026) and different catch-up amounts ($4,000 generally; $5,250 for ages 60–63). The $24,500 figure is for a traditional or safe harbor 401(k).
- Starter 401(k) deferral-only arrangements have their own limit ($6,000 for 2026, plus $1,100 for age 50+).
- The §415(c) annual-additions limit ($72,000 for 2026) and the annual compensation limit ($360,000 for 2026) are separate ceilings and do not change the $24,500 answer.

OPERATIONAL NOTES FOR THE PLAN

- $24,500 is the statutory maximum, not a floor. A plan document may impose a lower deferral cap (for example, a percentage-of-pay limit), and the plan's lower cap governs the participant. Confirm the plan's own deferral percentage/dollar cap before communicating a payroll figure.
- The limit is a calendar-year limit. Payroll must monitor year-to-date deferrals across the plan year, and for a participant who transferred from another employer's 401(k) during 2026, must obtain the prior plan's year-to-date deferral total to test the aggregated $24,500.
- Excess deferrals (amounts above $24,500, disregarding eligible catch-up) are includible in gross income for the year deferred and, if not corrected timely, are taxed again on distribution. Plans should have payroll controls verifying the §402(g) limit, with correction by distribution of excess deferrals plus allocable earnings.

SCOPE

US federal (IRS) rules only; assumes the employee is a standard participant in a traditional or safe harbor 401(k) and is asking for the base elective deferral limit excluding catch-up contributions. State law, non-US regimes, and plan-specific lower caps are outside this figure.
